issues.legal_issue: A public authority rejecting the highest tender must make sufficient reasons for its decision available and ordinarily communicate them to the affected tenderers.
material_facts: A government company acting as a development authority invited tenders for specified plots and rejected the appellants’ highest offers.
The tender scheme reserved a discretion to reject any or all offers without assigning reasons.
The authority stated that it had acted bona fide in seeking better offers; the Court did not apply its reasons requirement to the appeals, which failed.
issues.conclusion: When a public authority rejects the highest offer of this kind, it must make available reasons sufficient to indicate its position and ordinarily communicate them to the affected parties, unless there is a specific justification for not doing so. The Court did not apply that test to these appeals.
issues.legal_principle: The need for reasons in public decision-making supports transparency, accountability, administrative and judicial review, and the public’s interest in knowing about public transactions. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975) 4 SCC 428 and its discussion of expanding judicial review of administrative action.

predicates.public_authority_tender_case: A public authority invited tenders for the disposal of property.
predicates.highest_offer_rejected: The public authority rejected the highest offer received in response to its tender.

issues.definition: When a public authority rejects the highest tender, it must make reasons available and ordinarily communicate them, unless a specific justification supports not communicating them.

issues.legal_issue: A state instrumentality dealing with the public in a commercial activity remains subject to the rule against arbitrary action and to judicial review.
material_facts: The respondent was a government company constituted as a development authority and empowered to dispose of land vested in it.
The authority rejected the appellants’ highest offers under a tender scheme that reserved discretion to reject offers.
The Court treated the respondent as an instrumentality of the State dealing with citizens.
issues.conclusion: The authority was required to act within the rule of law, could not act arbitrarily in its dealings with the public, and was subject to judicial review despite the commercial nature of its activity.
issues.legal_principle: Article 12 of the Constitution encompasses the respondent as an instrumentality of the State, and Article 14 requires non-arbitrary state action. The Court relied on R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India (1979) 1 SCR 1042 and Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi, among other decisions.

predicates.state_instrumentality: The body making the decision was an instrumentality of the State.
predicates.public_authority_dealing_with_citizens: The body made a decision in the course of dealing with members of the public.

issues.definition: When a state instrumentality makes a decision while dealing with the public, it must act non-arbitrarily and remains subject to judicial review.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority disposing of property may seek a better economic return rather than accept the highest offer.
material_facts: The authority rejected the appellants’ highest offers for specified plots.
There was no allegation of mala fides in the authority’s refusal to accept those offers.
The Court proceeded on the basis that the authority sought better offers in the economic interests of the authority.
issues.conclusion: The State is entitled to seek the best deal for its property, and the authority’s bona fide pursuit of better offers could justify not accepting the highest offers, subject to the requirement to make reasons available.
issues.legal_principle: The State may seek the best return for its property; the Court noted that this approach had been accepted in decisions concerning state action under excise laws. This discretion remains subject to the requirements of non-arbitrary public action and giving reasons for rejection of the highest offer.

predicates.public_authority_property_disposal: A public authority was disposing of property.
predicates.bona_fide_search_for_better_return: The authority sought better offers for the economic benefit of the public body and its action was not alleged to be mala fide.

issues.definition: A public authority disposing of property may seek a better offer than the highest bid when it is bona fide pursuing a better economic return.
